stories.title: David-Horodok’s fires brought the town together to build a brigade
stories.why: Repeated fires were serious enough to prompt residents to establish a firefighters’ association, making communal self-organization part of town life.
stories.markdown:
![David-Horodok on the Horyn River](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg/1920px-%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)
## A town that prepared for fire

In David-Horodok, fire was not a distant danger but a recurring threat to ordinary life. The memorial book, in JewishGen’s translation, describes a town of wooden houses and thatched roofs where fire could return “almost every summer.” A hot iron left outside, a torch carried to a stable at night, an unextinguished cigarette, children playing with fire—or arson—could set a blaze in motion. Wind and closely packed combustible roofs could turn a mishap into a catastrophe. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav375.html))

Summer was a season of beauty and activity, but the danger changed how families lived. Some carried valuables to the town’s few brick houses; others kept belongings packed for a quick escape. One recollection makes the threat part of family chronology: the narrator’s mother used [the Great Fire](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_ffaa51036bca0a86af298030) to mark the time of his birth. The passage does not give a year, so it cannot securely identify that fire with the later blaze of 1936.

Another memory reaches further back. The [head of the kahal](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_ff9dd6d63a16afd17ca4405b) reportedly recalled a substantial fire in 1868. The memorial book presents community inquiries into the Great Fire’s date, but the evidence supplied here does not settle when it occurred. These accounts preserve how fires served as markers in local memory without allowing us to make one event out of every remembered blaze. The town stood in [Polesia](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a6cfefdf02483d0a9aecb8d6), a region whose wooded landscape and small settlements formed the wider setting of life, but the book’s account is specifically about the hazards faced in David-Horodok.

## Founders and a shared undertaking

After numerous fires, residents organized a formal response. The memorial book dates the [David-Horodok Firefighters Association](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1a77e56df6486c4ebcd2b349)’s founding to 1904; the separate event record gives the same year. The organization was not the work of one community alone. Jewish founders named in the book include Zeev Yudovitz and his son Bezalel, Mordecai (Moche) Rimer, Nisan Gorvitz, and Liba Fridman. The non-Jewish founders included Captain Tzereiski and Petrushkevitz. Tzereiski became the first commander and Petrushkevitz the secretary. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

The first contribution was practical and immediate: Zeev Yudovitz gave the organization his private well and two barrels. Jewish and non-Jewish residents also donated, and an insurance society in Minsk provided money for equipment. The account makes the brigade an example of shared local self-protection: fires threatened the whole town, and the response drew on residents and institutions beyond one household or group.

The memorial book names the people behind the association, but it does not explain all their family connections. It identifies Bezalel as Zeev’s son, for example, and lists Rimer and Gorvitz among the founders; it does not establish whether every similarly named person in other records belongs to these same families. The book also notes that Zeev built the Great Study House, but the brief evidence here does not show that this civic role and his firefighting contribution were part of the same undertaking.

## Equipment, training, and public life

The organization grew from donated water and barrels into a lasting civic institution. In 1911–1912, when Tzereiski was sent to the front, Rimer took command, assisted by Bezalel Yudovitz and Nisan Gorvitz. In 1919, the book says, Bezalel was murdered and Gorvitz became ill; Yosef Yudovitz and Simcha Mishalov replaced them. Petrushkevitz remained secretary until 1920, when Aharon Moravchik took over. These changes show how the brigade depended on successive local leaders, even as war and personal loss affected its ranks. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

By the time the Poles entered in 1920, the association had five pumps and eighteen barrels, along with other equipment. During the Polish period, two benzene motors and long rubber hoses were added. Its building grew, and a theater shared the premises; its proceeds helped fund firefighting. In 1937 a 25-meter tower with a siren was erected beside it. When an alarm sounded, 35 wagon drivers were summoned with their horses to carry people and equipment. The memorial book counts 63 volunteer firefighters, ten of them Poles. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

Training became a public ritual as well as preparation. In summer, the station watchman Massey walked the streets sounding a special bugle. Firefighters gathered in uniform, exercised, and staged a mock blaze at a house selected by one of their number. The recollection even preserves the drill’s comic edge: sometimes they chose the home of someone against whom they held a grudge. The townspeople watched; afterward, the firefighters shared beer. Such details make visible the association’s place in everyday life—not only as emergency equipment, but as a body of young people who practiced together and were recognized by their neighbors.

## The 1936 fire—and the limits of the defense

After the First World War, the brigade expanded. The town council increased its equipment and supported instruction in extinguishing fires and, especially, preventing them from spreading. The memorial book’s account of everyday life says almost all Jewish young people enrolled, regarding service as a civic obligation. Yet it also notes a disparity: although Christian residents’ thatched roofs faced particular danger, only three or four Christians joined the brigade. A separate account emphasizes that the fire department served the whole town and was the only Jewish-operated institution to receive a municipal subsidy. Together, these recollections show both broad community service and uneven participation. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav375.html))

The limits of the brigade became clear in 1936. According to the memorial book, a fire broke out in the middle of the day in the Christian part of town. Wind and nearby thatched roofs helped it spread beyond the firefighters’ ability to contain it. One account says one third of the town burned, including the Greek Orthodox church on the hill. Another memorial-book passage labels an image “The large fire of 1936 in David-Horodok.” These are accounts of the same dated catastrophe, but the supplied evidence does not give a more exact count of destroyed homes or independently verify the fraction of the town lost. The fire was a disaster, not proof that the association had failed: the book records both the brigade’s extensive preparations and the conditions under which it could not stop a blaze. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

The memorial book carries the brigade’s story into the years before the Second World War. In 1935, command passed from the aging Rimer to Simcha Mishalov; in 1937 Yosef Kozak replaced Mishalov, assisted by Yosef Yudovitz, Mishalov, and Yaakov Matosvitz. The association continued until the Red Army entered. By 1938 it had financed a brick theater, replacing an earlier wooden one, and its firefighters sometimes traveled to extinguish fires in nearby villages. The alarm tower, volunteers, wagons, pumps, theater, and shared donations tell one story: recurring danger pushed residents to build an organized response, while the 1936 blaze showed that collective effort could reduce vulnerability without mastering fire.

The independent record is thinner on this particular story. Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos identifies David-Horodok under the names Dawidgródek, Davyd-Haradok, and David-Gorodok, but its entry does not discuss the fire brigade or the 1936 fire. Virtual Shtetl’s town page confirms the place and its variant names, but likewise adds no independent account of the association or blaze. I found no relevant fire-brigade account in the searched YIVO or USHMM results. Thus the brigade’s founding, named organizers, equipment, and great fire remain documented here through the community’s own memorial book, not independently corroborated by those archives. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224))

## Sources

### From the memorial book

- [The Firefighters Organization of David-Horodok — Yosef Yudovitz, JewishGen translation](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html)
- [Firefighters and everyday life in David-Horodok, JewishGen translation](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav375.html)

### Independent sources

- [Yad Vashem, Encyclopedia of the Ghettos: Dawidgródek](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224)
- [Virtual Shtetl: Dawidgródek](https://sztetl.org.pl/pl/miejscowosci/d/985-dawidgrodek)

stories.title: David-Horodok’s revolution, pogrom threats, and the Balakhovtsy violence
stories.why: Revolutionary politics and repeated threats of violence tested the community while spurring political activity and efforts to protect residents.
stories.markdown:
## A political awakening in a small town

The story remembered in the memorial book is not one event on a single day, but a turn in the life of the [David-Horodok Jewish community](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1ffa438353dc176e94f25c7d): political organizing and hope, followed by threats of pogrom and, years later, armed violence. In the book’s account, revolutionary ideas reached this town on the Horyn River, where young people began gathering, arguing, and imagining a different future.

The memorial book’s witnesses describe the 1905 upheaval as a time when the old authority of the wealthy weakened and young people debated among themselves. One recollection names the Esserists, Iskrists, and Bundists—political tendencies whose ideas entered local discussions. Another describes the creation of a small Bund group in 1905, led by a man remembered as Helfant. A later passage identifies him as A. Litvak, “the crooked elephant,” and recalls students’ speeches, an illegal library, and secret gatherings. The book also says that revolutionary youth learned songs, parade practices, and the use of firearms near the Jewish cemetery. These accounts establish local organizing, but offer no precise chronology for each activity.

The memorial book itself acknowledges how limited its evidence is: its account of 1905 relies on memories, including those of people who had not taken an active part in the events. It also recalls that Helfant was taken away by sleigh under police guard, to a distant prison or Siberia; the precise destination is not established in the passage. After revolutionary hopes failed, some activists were arrested or left town, and many young people emigrated. One witness says that, except for [Mordechai Laptchevan](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_8a60d3d62d765bdd713fd4a2), who refused to leave, the “brothers and sisters” began departing. The book connects this exodus to the town’s subsequent impoverishment.

## Pogrom threats and Jewish self-defense

The danger was not only political repression. The memorial book remembers a strong and active local [Black Hundred organization](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_043013d7311062167cd5d468), loyal to tsarist authority and opposed to revolution. It says that the group attempted to organize a pogrom on a Sunday. The witnesses do not give a calendar date, and the accounts vary in emphasis: one says the attempt ended with a few Jewish people wounded; another mentions injuries without specifying a number.

The book credits the response to a Jewish youth self-defense organization, supported by the wider Jewish population, and also to the opposition of the town’s magistrate, Avtchinkov, who had business dealings with Jews. The account does not identify the self-defense organizers or describe their weapons, numbers, or actions in detail. It does, however, preserve an important point: residents did not face the threat only as isolated households. Young people organized, the broader community stood with them, and a local official’s intervention is remembered as part of why the attempted pogrom did not become a larger massacre.

These recollections should not be collapsed into a single precise incident. A separate account mentions reported preparations for a pogrom and the organization of a guard, while another says Black Hundreds tried to arrange attacks and caused injuries. The available passages do not establish whether these are different stages of the same threat or separate episodes. The memorial book’s memory is clear about fear and resistance, but not about an exact date or a complete sequence.

## The Balakhovtsy enter the town

The later violence came amid the military upheavals of 1921. Here, too, the memorial book’s accounts differ on timing. One says the Balakhovtsy entered David-Horodok during Shemini Atzeret; another places their arrival on the night of Hoshana Rabba, with the Bolshevik retreat occurring during the intermediate days of Sukkot. A separate memorial-book passage about a double murder names Simchat Torah in 1920. These dates and descriptions cannot safely be merged into a single exact chronology: the witnesses may be recalling different events or using different calendar markers. The supplied record describes the double murder as the killing of Aharon Hershel Dorzin and Shalom Boir, but the other quoted accounts do not provide those names.

The narrative of the Balakhovtsy’s arrival is stark. People—especially young people and women—hid indoors. The first victims in one account were Rabbi Dudle and Motle, a shopkeeper who had gone early to pray at the synagogue. Soldiers then raided homes and beat Jewish residents. Some troops were quartered in Jewish houses; families hoped that feeding soldiers might protect their homes from others, and the memorial book says this sometimes worked. In other houses, soldiers inspected valuables and later took them themselves or sent others to steal them. The final night before the troops went to the front was remembered as especially severe, with casualties, sexual violence against women, and widespread looting.

The book gives no complete victim list and no reliable total for those harmed. One later recollection says the number of victims in David-Horodok was relatively smaller than in other towns, but emphasizes that there were victims. It describes the town’s rescue in those days as owing chiefly to Reb Asher, son of Reb Yitzchak Berman. Another account recalls that residents appealed to the Polish military authorities, but the few officers present either could not or would not help. The difference between these accounts matters: the community’s survival is remembered both through the actions of a named local figure and through the limits of outside protection.

## What the town carried forward

Across these episodes, self-defense did not mean safety. In 1905, residents and youth organization helped prevent an attempted pogrom from becoming a larger disaster. During the Balakhovtsy occupation, residents tried to shield households, sought help from Polish officers, and endured assaults and robbery. The memorial book’s account of the soldiers’ departure describes a further threat: a detachment returned, arrested Rabbi Ravinski and other Jews, and demanded a ransom of 100,000 rubles within two hours. The rabbi was released to collect money and valuables. The passage portrays the community’s contribution—rings, chains, watches, and other possessions—as the price of freeing those held.

The political awakening of 1905 and the later violence were not the same event, nor does the book prove a direct line from one to the other. What it preserves is a community repeatedly forced to judge who might protect it: organized youth, neighbors, a magistrate, a rabbi, or an unreliable military authority. Its testimony is incomplete and sometimes inconsistent about dates, but it names both the danger and the people who tried to meet it.

Independent-source check: the searches located no independent Yad Vashem, USHMM, or YIVO account of the specific David-Horodok pogrom attempt or Balakhovtsy violence. The available Wikipedia article provides general town context but does not corroborate these events; it is not independent confirmation of the memorial book’s testimony. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok?utm_source=openai))

stories.title: David-Horodok’s 1917 opening: a community elects, learns, and celebrates
stories.why: The political opening after the February Revolution enabled new democratic community institutions and a visible flowering of Hebrew education and civic activity.
stories.markdown:
![David-Horodok, the town at the center of the 1917 events](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg/1920px-%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A brief opening in a time of upheaval

In 1917, revolution seemed to make a different kind of Jewish public life possible in [David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_70ddf47dab3327f5d8436ee6). The memorial book remembers the year not as one isolated event but as a sudden expansion of communal activity: elections, schooling, a library, and public celebrations. Its accounts also make clear how fragile that opening was. Authority changed repeatedly, and institutions founded in hope had little time to establish themselves.

The book’s accounts associate the first democratic election for the Jewish community with the February Revolution and the period after the Kerensky Revolution. One account says the election took place in 1917 on the initiative of the [Zionist Organization](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_fd6ce3ce35fbee98e208de16); another describes the election of a [community committee](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1804f3dcb827dc7d758649ed) after the Kerensky Revolution. These are related descriptions of the same opening, not evidence for two separate elections. The book also says that the newly chosen communal body could not accomplish much before the Bolshevik Revolution and wartime transfers of power disrupted it. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav036.html?utm_source=openai))

A more detailed election narrative appears elsewhere in the memorial book. It describes an electoral committee, a voter list, and three competing lists: Zionists, Poalei Zion, and non-partisans. The disagreements were not merely about personalities. They concerned what the community should be responsible for: the General Zionists promised attention to both secular and religious needs, while Poalei Zion argued for separating religious affairs from communal administration. The account says eight administrators were elected, but the council was invalidated before its opening meeting after the Bolsheviks took power. This added detail gives the election political substance while underscoring its short life. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html?utm_source=openai))

## Institutions for a new generation

Public life also took shape in education. The memorial book dates the opening of a Hebrew school to 1917, after the February Revolution. It names Manievitch as its leader and identifies Y. Zeldin, R. Shaffer, Y. Kashtan, and Y. Margolin among the teachers who helped establish it. The school was more than a classroom: Hebrew education gave local organizers a way to make a shared cultural future tangible to children and families.

The [Zionist Library](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_b059da0e0f53cd30400df436), also founded in 1917 according to the book, offered another civic foothold. The book describes it as a place where people met and organized continuing activity. A later memorial-book account includes a photograph caption identifying the library’s 1917 administration and naming several members, including Yossel Moravchik, Asher Zager, Yoshke Friedman, Shalom Kvetny, and Bina Gorin. Taken together, the school and library suggest how the revolutionary moment was converted into everyday institutions—not only declarations, but places to teach, read, meet, and organize. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav375.html?utm_source=openai))

These names and roles should be read with care: the supplied records identify Manievitch and the teachers by abbreviated or transliterated names, and the memorial book does not provide enough here to establish their family connections or later lives. The evidence preserves their local work more clearly than their biographies.

## May Day in the streets and assembly hall

The celebration of May 1, 1917, brought the political opening into public view. The memorial book’s account calls it an unusually joyful day for the Jewish community, while describing a procession and ceremonies that crossed religious and communal boundaries. Preparations included a [Jewish-Christian Joint Committee](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_d3968404cc6af27d8e363a97), which arranged festivities and invited a nearby [Hussar Regiment](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_d8d3104bee4bbf16781e9954) and its orchestra to take part. The account describes the demonstration visiting both church and synagogue, with music including “La Marseillaise” and “Hatikvah.” These details belong to the memorial book’s recollection; they should not be mistaken for independent confirmation of each scene. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav001.html?utm_source=openai))

That evening, a festive assembly was held. [Anshel Zeitshik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a8c806be3af502161caf978a) spoke about friendship and brotherhood among peoples, and [Yesif Onushko](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_6fe1d67fab55aa16cad4b10b), a Christian resident, stood beside him. The book remembers the gesture as deeply moving to those present. It captures the hope of the moment, but also its precariousness: a celebration could express a vision of solidarity without guaranteeing that political conditions would sustain it.

## What the record can—and cannot—confirm

The memorial book is the source for the local sequence linking elections, Hebrew schooling, the library, and May Day. Its accounts vary in emphasis and detail, and the election narrative supplies specific party lists and elected names that the shorter event descriptions do not. The safest reconciliation is that a democratic communal election was attempted in 1917, alongside the founding of cultural institutions and public celebrations, but that revolutionary upheaval soon curtailed the council’s work.

Independent checking is limited. The [Wikipedia article on Davyd-Haradok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok) confirms the town’s identity and broad historical setting, but does not discuss these 1917 community elections, school, library, or May Day events. Searches of Yad Vashem and the USHMM’s public reference material did not yield an independent account of this particular local opening. Their silence does not disprove the memorial book’s testimony; it means the event is presently best documented through community memory rather than a corroborating outside narrative.

The 1917 opening therefore matters not because its institutions immediately secured lasting power, but because residents acted as if they could shape communal life themselves. They elected, taught, organized, and celebrated together. The same testimony that preserves that hope also records its limits: a council stopped before it could properly meet, while the wider period remained unsettled. The story is both an account of beginnings and a reminder that, in revolutionary times, beginnings could be brief.

## Sources

### From the memorial book
- [Political, Cultural and Organizational Institutions in David–Horodok](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Davyd-Horodok/dav036.html), memorial book in JewishGen’s translation.
- [History of David-Horodok, pages 1–35](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav001.html), memorial book in JewishGen’s translation.
- [Election account, pages 103–112](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html), memorial book in JewishGen’s translation.
- [Zionist institutions and library photograph](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav375.html), memorial book in JewishGen’s translation.

### Independent sources
- [Davyd-Haradok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok), Wikipedia. It provides town context but no account of the 1917 events described here.

stories.title: David-Horodok’s interwar institutions and the emigration of its people
stories.why: Banks, schools, libraries, political movements, and elections reveal a community building its institutions even as migration carried residents away.
stories.markdown:
## Rebuilding a communal life

After the Polish-Bolshevik war, Jewish life in [David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1ffa438353dc176e94f25c7d) began to rebuild amid economic hardship and political uncertainty. The memorial book recalls that organizations, parties, youth movements, cultural societies, and charitable institutions took shape, with young people bringing particular energy to their work. The account presents not one institution but a network: schools and libraries, political organizations, banks, and communal bodies that helped residents learn, debate, earn a living, and care for one another.

This revival followed years of upheaval. The memorial book says that the town’s earlier organizations had broken apart during war and revolution; some activists were arrested or fled, and others left during dangerous periods. After the fighting, education became an urgent concern. The [Tarbut School](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_b84fd472a05662a588932f2c) was reestablished in 1924, under the leadership of [R. Mishlov](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_81aae6d249451ac6c7461c05). The memorial book describes it as beginning with three classes and later expanding to seven, sustained largely by tuition and the commitment of teachers, parents, and supporters. It continued into 1940, though the Soviet takeover changed its language of instruction from Hebrew to Yiddish.

For young people drawn to Zionism and pioneering, [Z. S.](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_90bfa7569d261aea5affc727) founded [Ha-Halutz](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_737b792f28a95935681c5fc5) in David-Horodok in 1923, according to the memorial book. This founding is the focus of one record, which gives the year as 1923. The surviving account situates the movement within a wider political and cultural landscape: its organizations offered ways to prepare for life and work in the Land of Israel, while schools, libraries, and study groups helped sustain Hebrew and Jewish cultural life at home.

The book also describes earlier pioneering aspirations that met obstacles. Following the postwar upheaval, a group formed with the intention of immigrating to the Land of Israel, but the book says events there in 1921 halted aliyah and the group remained in town. That account helps explain why the 1923 founding of Ha-Halutz mattered locally: a movement could keep a collective aspiration alive even when departure was delayed. The memorial’s surviving passages do not give the names of Ha-Halutz’s founders or describe its full local program, so those details remain uncertain.

## Books, debate, and mutual support

In 1925, [Poalei Zion (T.S.)](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_0cecccf343d4802cd94c15a5) founded the [J. L. Peretz Library](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_af97ada338caf5e5f2cd423e), named for the writer [J. L. Peretz](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_0cc227bfee1981b8fa9f9bb7). It served adult readers; the Tarbut School had its own substantial student library. The memorial book describes readers, self-education groups, and amateur drama, a cultural life that crossed party lines and brought literature into public settings.

The library’s story also reveals how emigration reshaped local institutions. As many veteran activists made aliyah, the library faced a crisis. In 1935, a younger group took over its management. The memorial names [Kopel Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_2d04e4e0140e605f38164369), [Chaim Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_3cabaebbb40750afe844757a), [Chaim Farber](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_d3409091933429674f01d1ae), and [Zvi Shaklber](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_bc404a094ffb8f45f77d499b); its fuller account identifies Shaklber as the group’s head. The library revived, its readers grew in number, and new Yiddish, Hebrew, and Polish books were added. The record of the young group’s takeover thus marks both continuity and change: people left, but younger residents assumed responsibility for the institutions they had built.

Economic institutions were another part of communal life. The [Bank for Commerce](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a33219ea619a8861ed770e45) was founded in 1923 under the management of [M. Kvitni](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a837f9db7c7d649755b77503); the [People’s Bank](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_7fb72c45bdf0d2a4628559ff) followed in 1924 under [Sh. Papish](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1dbe71ab55fa2f175fe1336f). These are management roles in the source, not evidence that either man employed the other or founded the bank alone. The memorial book later contrasts the banks’ experience during the 1933–1935 economic crisis: it says the merchants’ institution was forced to interrupt normal activity, while the People’s Bank continued more cautiously and met its obligations.

Political representation was contested too. The memorial book records that Jewish community-council elections took place in 1928 under Polish authorities, but the surviving excerpt does not provide results or candidate names. It would be misleading to infer who won or what the vote meant for any particular party.

## Leaving, staying, and the meaning of departure

Emigration was not a single movement or a simple choice. The memorial book’s account links departures to the aftershocks of war, restricted opportunities, and economic strain. It describes Jews leaving for Argentina, Cuba, and Canada, while others sought to reach the Land of Israel. The book does not provide a complete list of emigrants or a total number, and it does not establish the later fate of every family. Its account is a community recollection, not a comprehensive register of everyone who left or survived elsewhere.

The records preserve several different scales of departure: a pioneering group whose plans were interrupted; veteran library activists who made aliyah; and broader migration overseas. These movements changed the town even as its institutions endured. The younger people who revived the library in 1935 inherited more than books: they took on a civic and cultural responsibility left vulnerable by the departure of experienced members. Meanwhile, Ha-Halutz and the Tarbut School represented distinct but connected ways of preparing young people for a Jewish future—one oriented toward pioneering and aliyah, the other toward Hebrew education and communal culture.

Outside sources offer only limited independent checks on this particular story. Wikipedia’s entry for Davyd-Haradok confirms the town’s interwar Polish setting and notes its later wartime destruction, but it does not independently verify the local founding dates, named organizers, library succession, or destinations described here. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok?utm_source=openai)) Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos result concerns a different town, Gródek Jagielloński, not David-Horodok; it therefore adds no independent evidence about these interwar institutions or departures. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=208&utm_source=openai)) The specific evidence for the school, banks, library, election, and migration in this account comes from the memorial book, in JewishGen’s translation—not from independent confirmation.

The people named in the records bring the institutional story into focus: organizers and managers, educators, library stewards, and young activists. Yet the record remains incomplete. It does not identify most emigrants or trace the families who left. The story worth carrying forward is therefore both one of cultural vitality and of dispersal: people built institutions for a community in place, while many also chose—or hoped—to make lives elsewhere.

stories.title: David-Horodok welcomes the Red Army, then lives under repression and occupation
stories.why: The change from Polish rule to Soviet power and then German occupation overturned civic life and ushered in arrests and persecution.
stories.markdown:
## A town caught between armies

In September 1939, David-Horodok was a Jewish town in eastern Poland, on the Horyn River. Germany had invaded Poland on September 1; as war approached, townspeople listened anxiously for news and worried about what might happen when German forces reached them. The memorial book recalls that Jewish residents hoped the Soviet advance would spare them from Nazi rule and from the antisemitic Polish government they had experienced. Their relief was real, but the choice before them was not between safety and danger: it was between authorities whose consequences they could not yet know. [The memorial book’s account of David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_bcbe8f6f5fb9a4059354cafb)

The [Red Army’s entry into David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_d018a1c641f62042c86f8001) followed the Polish withdrawal. The memorial book places the arrival on September 19, 1939, after Polish forces crossed the Horyn and destroyed the bridge; it describes a brief exchange of fire before Soviet soldiers crossed by pontoon. A second account in the book gives the Red Army’s entry as 6 a.m. that day. The accounts differ in emphasis and detail, so the precise sequence at the river should be read as remembered testimony rather than as a single independently verified minute-by-minute chronology. [A firefighter’s account in the memorial book, JewishGen’s translation](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a7a45f36af6961a2897defe5)

Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos identifies Dawidgródek—another form of the town’s name—as a prewar town in Poland’s Polesie district, and describes its Jewish community as numbering about 3,000 between the wars. Its account independently places the town in the wartime geography later shaped by German occupation. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224&utm_source=openai))

## The welcome—and what followed it

The memorial book describes a public welcome after the fighting ended: Jewish and non-Jewish residents came into the streets, smiling and greeting the Soviet troops. [The celebration of the Red Army’s arrival](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a7a45f36af6961a2897defe5) was led, in the book’s telling, by a small group of Jewish Communists and joined by other townspeople. Residents spoke with the soldiers about Polish rule and were encouraged by their accessibility and promises that Jews would no longer face the same troubles. The book remembers September 19 as a day of happiness and hope.

That welcome did not mean that Soviet rule left communal life untouched. The memorial book recalls that authorities prohibited Hebrew instruction, changing what children could learn at school. In one witness’s recollection, teacher Barentshuk struggled to tell pupils they would now study in Yiddish rather than Hebrew. The restriction threatened more than a curriculum: it struck at a language and educational tradition bound up with communal identity and hopes of emigration. [Barentshuk, the teacher named in the account](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_3cd0b3d6a10d6e71964c50a0)

The book also remembers residents who hoped to leave for the Land of Israel, and describes the new regime as narrowing those possibilities. That tension is important: the arrival was celebrated because it seemed to avert an immediate danger, while the Soviet authorities soon constrained institutions and choices the community valued. A wider historical account likewise states that the town came under Soviet control after the 1939 invasion of Poland and remained so until 1941. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok?utm_source=openai))

## Arrests and the prison in Pinsk

In February 1941, Soviet repression became personal and frightening. The memorial book records that ten activists were arrested during the night of February 10–11. [The arrest of ten activists](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a19e6f666e975c24f9e7299e) appears alongside another account of [arrests in the town on February 11](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_7059a3a853babd802d7e754c). Together, the records point to a nighttime roundup associated with political suspicion, but they do not establish that every detainee had the same affiliation or that the surviving accounts preserve a complete list.

Among the named detainees were Shmuel Zezik and Kopel Moravchik; the witness’s account connects their arrest to the political character of the imprisonment. Kopel Moravchik is also remembered as having later immigrated to Israel, though the supplied account does not establish his full family history or the details of his release. [Kopel Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_2d04e4e0140e605f38164369) Arrests and interrogation did not end in town: detainees were transferred to [Pinsk’s central prison](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_314da5c9a05391fc43662b46). The move from the local streets to a regional prison shows how state power reached into the community and removed people from their families and neighbors.

The memorial book names people from several strands of David-Horodok’s communal and political life, but the records supplied here do not give enough information to reconstruct their family relationships or the circumstances of every person’s fate. Shmuel Tschtschik, for example, is remembered as a party leader who helped reorganize branch activity; that does not, by itself, establish that he was among the February detainees. [Shmuel Tschtschik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_936d206e1ae600ad0d33ca9d) Likewise, Aharon Moravchik is named in connection with earlier political organization, but the supplied record does not establish a family relationship to Kopel. [Aharon Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_450655fb29af7fe167d8a78d)

## German occupation ends the Soviet interlude

When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, Soviet rule in David-Horodok was nearing its end. The memorial book says the Bolsheviks left in early July and German forces entered soon afterward. Its event record gives the occupation as July 1941; a separate chapter in the translated memorial book gives July 5, while Yad Vashem’s encyclopedia states that the Soviets withdrew on July 5. A Wikipedia town history gives German occupation as beginning July 7. These sources agree on the early-July transition but differ on the date of German entry; it would be misleading to turn them into a single precise date. [The German occupation of David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_b44aaba146a1460fdd8ee6f3)

The change of power was not a simple handover from one army to another. The memorial book recounts that, before German troops arrived, a local delegation went to the German authorities in Pinsk to urge their advance. This is the book’s account of local collaboration, not independent proof of the motives or conduct of every Christian resident. Yad Vashem’s town entry provides independent context for the German occupation and the destruction that followed, while the town history on Wikipedia also places the occupation in July 1941. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224&utm_source=openai))

The sequence remembered here—hope at the Red Army’s arrival, restrictions under Soviet rule, arrests and imprisonment, then German occupation—does not make the February arrests a direct cause of the Holocaust. It does show how rapidly the community’s security and autonomy narrowed. Under Soviet rule, activists could be seized and taken away; under German rule, the Jewish community faced a different and far more lethal persecution. The memorial book’s later chapters and independent records describe the town’s destruction, but this account stops at the transition into occupation rather than folding that later history into an event that began in 1939.

stories.why: The mass murder of the town’s Jews, the killing of those still hiding, and the discovery of an empty town at liberation mark the destruction of the community.
stories.markdown:
## The killings began with the men

The destruction of the [David-Horodok Jewish community](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1ffa438353dc176e94f25c7d) unfolded in stages: men were seized and murdered, women and children were driven from their homes, and the survivors were eventually confined in a ghetto and killed or forced to flee. The [memorial book’s accounts](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a79f8d2046f4576e040bfae9) preserve different dates and details; they do not yield one completely consistent chronology.

The first killings are remembered in one account as a July Aktion in which all the town’s men were murdered; another describes an early-August roundup. These may be different descriptions of the sequence, or differing recollections of its timing. The memorial book also records the killing of 53 people in 1941, including Jacob, Hannah’s father, and Gitl’s husband. That figure does not agree with the account describing thousands of victims, and the records do not explain whether the 53 refers to a separate incident.

The best-detailed account describes a mass killing of Jewish men aged fourteen and older. It says they were called to assemble under the pretext of forced labor, then marched to prepared graves near Hinavsk. Another account places the graves along the road between Chinovsk and Olshan. In the JewishGen translation, Michael Nosanchuk recalls hearing gunfire from Rubiel and dates the massacre to around the 16th of Av; the passage also gives August 10. A different memorial-book record gives August 16. The discrepancy should remain visible: the sources do not establish one uncontested Gregorian date or place.

Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos independently describes men aged fourteen and older being taken to pits near Olszany and murdered on August 10, 1941, by an SS cavalry unit. It records two children escaping and later reaching partisans. This broadly corroborates the memorial book’s account of the men’s murder, while differing from some of its date and location formulations. ([Yad Vashem, David-Horodok entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224))

## A town emptied, families scattered

The memorial book names local collaborators as well as victims. Its account identifies Maraiko—also rendered Mareyke—as a local authority figure, and describes Germans and local men participating in the roundup and killing. One passage says [Jacob ben Abba Gratsulin](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_b41daceebb9e1a15bf33afc2) alone had been told the fate awaiting those being taken away; he was shot while trying to escape. [Leyb Trayster](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_ff01ba7bdb3eaa9610db99ee) is remembered as leading a group left to arrange bodies before they too were murdered. These are names preserved in a community’s testimony, not a complete roster of the dead.

After the men’s killing, women and children were ordered out of town. Some fled toward nearby places, including Stolin, Sarny, and Lachwa; others returned or had nowhere safe to go. Yad Vashem likewise records that hundreds reached nearby towns, while many could not find shelter and returned to David-Horodok. The same source says a ghetto was established in early 1942, with women and children forming most of its population. ([Yad Vashem](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224))

The records also preserve individual attempts to survive. [Michael Nosentschuk’s escape](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_13a4ac26b31cc98227656ab9) was aided by a non-Jewish man who took him out of the ghetto. Another account tells of three hidden men—Kehat, Moses, and Abraham—murdered by non-Jews while traveling toward Stolin in 1943. Such stories show both the importance of flight and its terrible risks. The supplied records do not resolve the identities or later fates of every family member, nor do they provide a complete account of who escaped beyond the region.

## The ghetto’s last days

The memorial book describes a year of hunger, illness, and danger in the ghetto. One witness recalls a mother washing and dressing in clean clothes as she prepared for death on what she understood to be the final night. The passage is a stark record of fear, but it does not by itself establish the exact fate of her parents.

Yad Vashem provides a more precise account of the ghetto’s liquidation: on September 9, 1942, it says, 1,263 people remained, only 30 of them men. The ghetto was liquidated the following day; approximately 1,100 people were murdered at the killing site used for the men, while about 100 escaped, some joining Soviet partisan units. ([Yad Vashem](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224)) The memorial book’s broader account likewise says that women and children were taken to the earlier killing place and shot, but does not give this same precise date and count.

The account leaves important questions open: the identities of the two children who escaped the first massacre, the woman partisan whose name and fate were not preserved, and the later paths of those who reached the forest. A town-wide story cannot restore every missing biography. The memorial book records survivors’ memories, but, as a work written by survivors, it cannot be treated as a complete register of all families or fates.

## Liberation without return

The Red Army liberated David-Horodok in 1944. The memorial book says that no living Jews were found in the town. The record of liberation is therefore not a story of a community returning home: it marks the end of occupation after the Jewish town had already been destroyed.

Some survivors visited afterward and found the town burned. A memorial-book account mentions Hershl Karman and his sons in connection with such a visit, though the wording does not clearly establish that every one of them was among the visitors. A separate account describes partisans burning Jewish houses so that local residents would not benefit from Jewish property. These memories point to a landscape stripped of homes as well as people, but do not establish the fate of every building or survivor.

The Independent sources found here add useful checks but remain limited. Yad Vashem’s ghetto encyclopedia corroborates the main sequence and supplies dates and figures that the memorial book’s witnesses do not consistently agree on. A general entry on Davyd-Haradok likewise summarizes the occupation and killings, but is not a separate witness account. ([Davyd-Haradok, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok)) No town-specific article on this event was located in the YIVO Encyclopedia or the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia in the searches conducted. The memorial book remains essential for the named people and remembered experiences; the gaps and disagreements are part of the record, not a license to fill them with certainty.
